name: Sie
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file

new_statements.quote: Primary stress is almost invariably found on the penultimate syllable. In words of four syllables or more, a secondary stress attaches to the preceding syllable but one. ... Thus: ['nvat] 'stone', ['movoy] 'outrigger pole', [na'lintoŋ] 'lobster', [ˌsesi'maŋsi] 'index finger'. It should be noted that stress assignment occurs after all morphophonemic processes have applied. This means that stress does not necessarily attach to root syllables only, as affixed syllables can also be stressed. Syllabic material that is inserted or deleted morphophonemically within roots is also counted in the normal way for stress assignment purposes.
new_statements.citation: Crowley, Terry. 2002. Sye. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds), The Oceanic Languages, 694-722. Richmond: Curzon.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the surface word (monosyllables stressed on their only vowel); stress is computed on the output of all morphophonemic processes, so suffixes and inserted/deleted syllables count and affixal syllables can bear stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Crowley 2002: in words of four or more syllables, secondary stress on the syllable two before the primary (i.e. alternating leftward, e.g. [ˌsesi'maŋsi]). Lynch & Capell 1983 p. 22 instead place secondary stress on the initial syllable of words of more than three syllables (['orutenmoŋi]); Lynch 2001 p. 9: 'normally two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: Crowley: 'almost invariably' penultimate (no list given in the sketch). Lynch & Capell 1983 pp. 21-22: 'a handful of words with stress on the final syllable' (Capell's MS recorded some irregularly final-stressed nouns such as breadfruit [nmar] < nemar, which Lynch links to pretonic vowel loss); epenthetic schwa/copy vowels breaking heterorganic consonant clusters are never stressed and are not counted as syllables for stress assignment ([nov(ə)'laimp(ə)ɣon] 'its tail').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated over inflected surface words including affixes (Crowley's examples are affixed verb forms [ɣ-o'roŋ-yau] '(s)he heard me', ['ɣ-orŋ-oŋ], [ɣo'ɣ-orŋ-i]); examples are citation forms; no phrase-level discussion. No vowel-length contrast in Sye (unlike Tanna/Anejom where long final vowels attract stress).
new_statements.identity_note: All three modern sources describe the same language under two spellings: Sie (Lynch & Capell 1983) and Sye (Crowley 1998/2000/2002), glottocode siee1239, ISO erg, the modern language of Erromango. Crowley 2002 is an abridgment of Crowley 1998, based largely on speaker Edward Nalial. Lynch 2001's 'Erromango' generalisation covers Sye and moribund Ura (urav1235) together.

sources.citation: Lynch, John & A. Capell. 1983. Sie grammar outline. In John Lynch (ed.), Studies in the languages of Erromango, 11-74. Pacific Linguistics C-79. Canberra: ANU. [sec. 1.5 Stress, pp. 21-22]
sources.note: Sec. 1.5 pp. 21-22: 'Apart from a handful of words with stress on the final syllable, primary stress in Sie falls on the vowel of a monosyllable and the penultimate vowel of a polysyllable'; epenthetic vowels breaking heterorganic clusters are not stressed and not counted; 'Secondary stress occurs on the initial syllable of words of more than three syllables'. p. 21 also notes Capell's MS recorded some (irregular) final-stressed forms.

sources.citation: Lynch, John. 2001. The linguistic history of Southern Vanuatu. Pacific Linguistics 509. Canberra: ANU. [sec. 1.5.2 p. 9; ch. 4 Proto Southern Vanuatu stress pp. 101-117]
sources.note: p. 9: 'Primary stress is invariably on the penultimate syllable in Erromango. In Anejom and the Tanna languages, it is normally penultimate, but (a) final if the vowel of the final syllable is long, and (b) antepenultimate in certain very restricted contexts. Secondary stress normally occurs two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable.' Ch. 4 reconstructs PSV stress (penultimate if final syllable open, final if closed) - historical.
